variables.label: Scale
variables.help: the level at which the study examines AI's effects, by the primary unit of analysis and the level at which outcomes and conclusions are analysed, not by sample size or setting: a large sample of individual workers is micro; meso only when organisational outcomes are directly examined; macro only when aggregate labour-market or economic outcomes are studied; with several levels, the primary level of the empirical analysis

options.label: Micro
options.definition: effects on individuals or small teams: worker productivity, behaviour, skills, task performance, also when the participants work within firms or across several organisations

options.label: Meso
options.definition: effects on organisations, firms, workplaces or organisational structures: firm-level productivity, staffing, workflows, organisational performance

options.label: Macro
options.definition: effects on labour markets, industries, regions or entire economies: aggregate employment, wages, occupational demand, economy-wide productivity

variables.label: Research design
variables.help: the study's overall empirical design, by how AI exposure is assigned and how the study is organised, for the paper's main with-versus-without-AI comparison; a paper whose tasks differ in design takes the main comparison's, the others noted in task_notes; the estimator goes in identification_strategy

options.label: Lab RCT
options.definition: participants randomly assigned to AI conditions in a controlled, in-person setting

options.label: Online RCT
options.definition: participants randomly assigned in an online experiment or web-based setting

options.label: Field RCT
options.definition: participants randomly assigned in a real workplace or market

options.label: Natural experiment
options.definition: AI exposure arises from an external event or plausibly exogenous variation outside the researchers' control: a launch, a rollout, a policy

options.label: Observational
options.definition: naturally occurring AI use or exposure analysed without experimental assignment and without an exogenous event; identification_strategy says how the comparison is made

options.label: Descriptive
options.definition: describes AI use or outcomes without a treatment or exposure comparison

options.label: other
options.definition: none of the categories fits: give the paper's own term in `proposed`

variables.label: Identification strategy
variables.help: the primary method used to identify or estimate the causal effect of AI exposure in the main comparison: the actual estimation method, not a broad label such as natural experiment; a specific strategy over generic regression adjustment

options.label: Random assignment
options.definition: causal effects identified through randomized treatment assignment

options.label: Difference in differences
options.definition: changes in outcomes between treated and comparison groups before and after AI exposure, staggered adoption designs included

options.label: Regression discontinuity
options.definition: effects identified at a treatment-assignment threshold

options.label: Instrumental variable
options.definition: an instrument that shifts AI exposure but is assumed not to affect outcomes directly

options.label: Interrupted time series
options.definition: changes in outcome levels or trends after the AI's introduction, from repeated observations over time

options.label: Matching
options.definition: comparable treated and untreated groups constructed on observed characteristics

options.label: Regression adjustment
options.definition: statistical controls for observed confounders without a more specific identification strategy

options.label: Pre/post
options.definition: outcomes before and after AI adoption without an untreated comparison group

options.label: None
options.definition: no causal identification strategy is implemented

options.label: other
options.definition: none of the categories fits: give the paper's own term in `proposed`

options.label: Writing
options.definition: Producing new prose text from scratch. E.g., drafting a cover letter, press release or essay.

options.label: Editing & Feedback
options.definition: Improving existing text or work, or giving written feedback on it. E.g., revising a draft for clarity, giving peer feedback on an essay.

options.label: Summarizing & synthesis
options.definition: Condensing or integrating given source material into a shorter account that stays faithful to the sources. E.g., summarizing a report, synthesizing findings from several papers.

options.label: Translation

options.label: Programming

options.label: Data analysis

options.label: Information search

options.label: Problem solving & reasoning

options.label: Classification & detection
options.definition: Assigning items to predefined categories. E.g., labelling X-rays as normal/abnormal, flagging fake news.

options.label: Evaluation & selection
options.definition: Judging the quality of items or choosing among options, where no predefined category scheme exists. E.g., screening CVs, grading essays, picking an investment.

options.label: Forecasting
options.definition: Predicting future outcomes or unknown quantities. E.g., predicting recidivism, forecasting sales.

options.label: Ideation

options.label: Persuasion & negotiation

options.label: Physical & manual tasks

variables.label: Knowledge & education (evidence)
variables.help: what a person had to already know to do this at all: domain and level, scaffolding provided, what they still had to bring. Describe; do not score

variables.label: Goal & path (evidence)
variables.help: how a solver would work out how to proceed: route obvious or discovered, one right answer or many, could one commit to a wrong route and fail; the objective and the done-state. Describe; do not score

variables.label: Interdependence (evidence)
variables.help: the internal structure of the work: parts of different kinds or one repeated unit; feedback while working; would an early mistake surface during the work or only at the end. Describe; do not score

variables.label: Resources & context (evidence)
variables.help: what a participant had to have or find beyond the instructions: documents, a codebase, data, tools, the internet, firm- or study-specific knowledge; handed over or to be supplied. Do not count the AI tool. Describe; do not score

variables.label: Task notes
variables.help: what a coder must know about the task: what participants did when the name does not say it, how arms map to the paper's conditions, a design that differs from the study's design_type, in a reversed design the worker the AI replaces, discrepancies

variables.label: Knowledge & education: complex?
variables.help: Knowledge and Education: is the task complex on this dimension? Yes or No by the rubric (the options carry the criteria); mark in the PDF the sentences the score rests on. If scaffolding substantially lowered the bar (worked examples, cheat-sheets, procedure-recall tools), score based on what participants actually had to bring after the scaffolding. Programming note: it is the depth of programming knowledge that matters, not the language name. Intro courses teach Python, Java, or C — but professional uses often require more than basics to use these languages effectively. Do not score a language as first-year simply because it appears in introductory curricula.

options.label: Yes
options.definition: the task requires second-year undergraduate knowledge or above. That is at least some degree of specialization within knowledge domain.

options.label: No
options.definition: high-school or first-year undergraduate knowledge suffices, including basic undergraduate concepts.

variables.label: Goal & path: complex?
variables.help: Goal Definition and Path Specification: is the task complex on this dimension? Yes or No by the rubric (the options carry the criteria); mark in the PDF the sentences the score rests on. Subjective or holistic grading is evidence of openness but not sufficient on its own — a concrete problem with an easy-to-infer route, rated holistically (e.g. "resolve this customer's issue," scored by CSAT), is still No. A clean outcome metric does not make a task closed if the route to it is hard to infer.

options.label: Yes
options.definition: the path to completion is hard to infer: it is not obvious how to proceed from the stated objective, OR there are many valid approaches / no single right answer, so it is easy to get lost or commit to a wrong route. Importantly, in getting lost there should be a mistake that makes the task fail. This includes tasks whose end-state and metric are perfectly clear but whose route is undiscovered and tasks where it is hard to identify what the objective even is. For example "improve firm profit," "get rich," "win the game", are all tasks whose route is hard to discover and the wrong path would cause a failure (e.g. company default or losing the game).

options.label: No
options.definition: how to proceed is easy to infer, even if the instruction does not spell it out: a determinate done-state with an obvious or readily-found route and little risk of getting lost (a defined deliverable against a key or rubric, a specific problem with a specified target).

variables.label: Interdependence: complex?
variables.help: Task Interdependence: is the task complex on this dimension? Yes or No by the rubric (the options carry the criteria); mark in the PDF the sentences the score rests on. Three rules: - Trivial decomposition is not interdependence. "You must do A before B" holds almost everywhere and is not the target. Score Yes only when the parts are of different nature and an early error is genuinely hard to spot and costly to undo. - Easy, timely correction defeats coupling. Fast, reliable feedback (a counterpart who corrects you, a rerunnable test, visible intermediate results) → No. Slow, noisy, or confounded feedback (a market signal weeks later) does not count. - Programming tasks: distinguish compile-time from deployment feedback. Compilers/tests catch syntax and unit-level errors quickly, but multi-day/multi-week projects surface the relevant feedback at integration or deployment — slow and noisy. A 1-hour task with a rerunnable test suite → No; an ongoing project where errors surface at launch or in downstream systems → Yes. - Do not score from the grading structure. A conjunctive grade ("pass all 12") or a single holistic score is a measurement property, not task structure; ignore it.

options.label: Yes
options.definition: the task combines genuinely *different* kinds of subtask, AND an error in an early or upstream component is *hard to catch as the work proceeds* and *likely to propagate or be costly to fix* — often forcing a partial restart rather than a local patch. The heart of the dimension is that mistakes are hard to detect mid-task and expensive to unwind, not that recovery is strictly impossible.

options.label: No
options.definition: the work is either (a) a stream of independent or repeated homogeneous units (one chat after another, paragraph after paragraph), where an error stays local; or (b) coupled but where errors are *easy to catch and cheap to fix as you go* — a counterpart redirects you, you rerun a test, you see intermediate output and revise before completion.

variables.label: Resources & context: complex?
variables.help: Resources and Context: is the task complex on this dimension? Yes or No by the rubric (the options carry the criteria); mark in the PDF the sentences the score rests on. Do not count the AI tool being studied as a resource — it is the treatment.

options.label: Yes
options.definition: the task requires substantial resources beyond what is handed to the participant: extensive materials to search or synthesise across a large context (e.g. a corpus of documents, multiple studies to browse, a large codebase, browsing the internet for at least an hour), specialist data sources or tools, or substantial context-specific knowledge — whether firm-specific (e.g. tacit knowledge), study-specific, procedural, or otherwise — that the participant must bring or that would need to be supplied to a model.

options.label: No
options.definition: the task is self-contained: a few materials sitting directly in front of the participant suffice, and it draws only on general knowledge or basic everyday tacit knowledge.

The specific category wins over the generic one; recruitment through an online platform or panel takes precedence over general_population whatever the age, nationality or demographic restrictions; never other merely because a sample is heterogeneous or distinctively described

variables.label: Expertise
variables.help: the arm's training and experience in the domain of the task, decided in this order: (1) people employed in the occupation the task belongs to are expert, whatever their seniority and whatever spread of skill or experience the paper reports among them, unless the paper itself calls them junior, then intermediate; (2) students in the field and trainees are intermediate; (3) people with no training in the domain (the general public, crowdworkers, job applicants, students outside the field) are novice; (4) mixed only when the arm deliberately combines people from different levels in this sense (students with professionals, laypeople with experts), never for a reported skill spread within one occupational sample; (5) not_applicable only for a task with no domain anyone could be trained in (a hidden-profile game, a generic survey); (6) not_stated when the paper says nothing about who the people are

options.label: Novice
options.definition: no training in the task domain: the general public, crowdworkers, job applicants, students outside the field; a sample described as needing no specific industry or contextual knowledge

options.label: Intermediate
options.definition: students in the field, trainees, and staff the paper itself calls junior

options.label: Expert
options.definition: employed in the occupation the task belongs to, whatever the seniority or the spread of skill the paper reports, unless the paper itself calls them junior

options.label: Mixed
options.definition: the arm deliberately combines people from different levels (students with professionals, laypeople with experts); a reported spread of skill or experience within one occupational sample is not mixed

options.label: Not applicable
options.definition: the task has no domain anyone could be trained in

options.label: not stated
options.definition: the paper gives no information on who the people are

variables.label: Representativeness
variables.help: how the arm's sample relates to a population

options.label: Population-wide
options.definition: e.g. register data in Denmark

options.label: representative sample
options.definition: e.g. household or firm survey

options.label: non-representative sample
options.definition: e.g. small experiment

variables.label: Countries
variables.help: where the arm's people or data come from, not the authors; 'online, unspecified' when the paper does not say

variables.label: People in the arm
variables.help: human subjects who did this task in this arm; null if not stated

variables.label: What this arm got
variables.help: tool, access, training, prompts, restrictions: what made this condition what it was

variables.label: Arm notes
variables.help: anything a coder must know about the arm

variables.label: AI model
variables.help: the exact system this arm used, with version and access route ('GPT-4 via ChatGPT Plus', 'GitHub Copilot', 'Claude Sonnet 4'); null for a no-AI reference arm or if not stated

variables.label: AI role
variables.help: how the AI took part in the work in this arm; none for a no-AI reference arm

options.label: Open-ended assistance
options.definition: the human has open-ended access and uses it however they like; a general-purpose chatbot or agent is open_ended_assistance
options.notes: How was AI used to solve the task?

options.label: AI review
options.definition: The human produces the work and AI provides feedback.

options.label: AI advice
options.definition: AI gives a recommendation like a prediction or a label but human makes decision. E.g. radiology image classification or algorithmic hiring

options.label: Human review
options.definition: AI produces the work and the human reviews it.

options.label: AI-only
options.definition: Full delegation with human limited to prompting, guiding and giving feedback.

options.label: none
options.definition: the arm did not use AI (a no-AI reference arm)

variables.label: Agentic tool
variables.help: whether the AI autonomously executes a multi-step task or workflow rather than merely responding or assisting: true when it independently determines and executes successive actions toward a goal (conducting an interview, navigating software, using tools, modifying files, completing a workflow with limited human intervention); false when it responds to individual prompts, generates content, recommends or assists without executing a sequence of actions on its own; null for a no-AI reference arm

variables.label: How AI enters
variables.help: how AI exposure or use is operationalised in this arm; null for a no-AI reference arm

options.label: exposure
options.definition: potential exposure to AI measured through an index, score or proxy based on tasks, occupations or capabilities, e.g. Eloundou et al.

options.label: adoption
options.definition: actual AI adoption or deployment by workers, firms or organisations, naturally occurring rollouts included, where adoption is not assigned by the researchers

options.label: observed usage
options.definition: actual intensity, frequency or patterns of AI use measured through usage logs, interactions or other behavioural records

options.label: experimental access
options.definition: the researchers assign, provide or withhold access to AI as part of an experimental intervention, whether or not the participants use it

variables.label: Outcome id
variables.help: O1, O2 … in the paper's order

variables.label: Measure
variables.help: the outcome as the paper names it: 'time taken', 'average grade'

variables.label: How measured
variables.help: who or what produced the measure and against what standard: blinded professional graders on a 1-7 rubric, self-reported minutes, a timer

variables.label: Unit
variables.help: the unit or scale of the measure as printed: 'minutes', '1-7 scale', 'percent correct', 'USD', 'count'; null when the paper gives none

variables.label: Better side
variables.help: up if higher values are better (quality, output); down if lower is better (time, errors); neutral for a quantity without a better side

variables.label: Outcome class
variables.help: what kind of outcome the measure is, by what was measured and not by its name; every outcome measured while the treatment arm has the AI in use, with a with-versus-without-AI contrast, is a row; an outcome measured afterwards without the AI (a post-test, a retention test, later unaided work) is not a row: name it in task_notes

options.label: work performance
options.definition: the work produced or the task performed, measured by graders, instruments, timers, counts or an answer key: time, output volume, quality, accuracy, errors, completion, creativity or novelty rated by others

options.label: behaviour
options.definition: what people did, observed: use or adoption of the AI, reliance on or acceptance of its suggestions, take-up of the assigned condition, time allocation across tasks, effort, help-seeking, collaboration

options.label: subjective report
options.definition: what people reported about themselves or the work: satisfaction, enjoyment, well-being, stress, perceived agency or autonomy, trust, confidence, self-assessed performance, beliefs, attitudes, intentions

options.label: labour market
options.definition: employment status, retention or attrition, earnings, hours, promotion, hiring

options.label: Task shift

options.label: Output diversity

options.label: Performance dispersion
options.definition: the spread of performance across people: a slope by baseline skill, a variance, a correlation across tasks

options.label: AI vs no AI
options.definition: an AI arm against a no-AI reference arm (concurrent or placebo tool)

options.label: post vs pre
options.definition: the same units after getting the AI against before

options.label: AI vs AI

options.label: treatment on the treated

options.label: not applicable

variables.label: Statistic
variables.help: what the central value in `mean` is

variables.label: n
variables.help: people (or units) behind this row's value

variables.label: Observations
variables.help: the observations behind the estimate when they differ from the people (tasks x participants, person-weeks, tickets), as printed; null when equal to n or not stated

variables.label: Clustered on
variables.help: what the standard errors are clustered on ('participant', 'team', 'branch'), as stated; null if not clustered or not stated

variables.label: Mean
variables.help: the arm's central value of the measure as printed, whichever statistic the paper gives (`statistic` says which); a proportion as printed (0.82 or 82, not converted)

variables.label: SD
variables.help: the arm's standard deviation as printed; from an SE or CI only with estimated = true and the arithmetic in result_notes; for a median, null with the IQR in result_notes

variables.label: Effect as reported
variables.help: the number exactly as printed, with its sign and unit: '-40%', '+0.41 SD', '0.18 (0.05)'; null on a reference-arm row

variables.label: Effect value
variables.help: the same number as a plain number in the units of effect_type; null if the paper gives only a direction

variables.label: Effect type
variables.help: the form of the number in effect_value

variables.label: Effect units
variables.help: 'minutes', 'percent of the control mean', 'SD of the pre-treatment grade', 'log points'

variables.label: SE
variables.help: standard error as printed

variables.label: CI low
variables.help: lower 95% bound as printed

variables.label: CI high
variables.help: upper 95% bound as printed

variables.label: p
variables.help: as a number, as printed; null if only stars or an inequality

variables.label: p as printed
variables.help: the significance exactly as printed when p_value cannot hold it: '<0.01', 'p = .03', '***' (with the note's star convention); null otherwise

variables.label: Estimated
variables.help: true if any value in the row was read from a figure or computed rather than printed; say how in result_notes

variables.label: Main estimate
variables.help: true for the paper's main specification of this measure: the estimate the results section leads with (the main table's full-sample row), not a robustness check, an alternative estimator or a secondary specification; at most one per estimand

variables.label: Source
variables.help: 'Table 2, column 3', 'Figure 1', 'p. 5 text'

variables.label: Outcome
variables.help: the id (O1 …) of the outcome in the coder's outcomes list

variables.label: Estimate
variables.help: the id of the model estimate this row was accepted from; empty for a row added by hand

variables.label: Result notes
variables.help: derivations, which specification, caveats
